content: Leukonychia is a medical term used to describe the presence of white discoloration on the nails. The term originates from the Greek words leuko, meaning white, and onyx, meaning nail. The most frequent cause of leukonychia is trauma to the nail matrix, which is the area at the base of the nail where nail growth occurs. Types of Leukonychia 1. Leukonychia Totalis: This condition involves the complete whitening of the nail. It can be associated with hypoalbuminemia (a condition characterized by low levels of albumin in the blood), certain genetic disorders, or as a side effect of sulphonamides, which are a class of antibiotics. 2. Leukonychia Partialis: This refers to partial whitening of the nail and can be further categorized into specific subtypes: Leukonychia Striata (Transverse Leukonychia): This presents as white bands or striations across the nail. It may result from conditions such as cirrhosis, chemotherapy, or physical trauma to the nail matrix, such as repetitive tapping or slamming the nail in a door. This condition can resemble Mee's lines, which are caused by heavy metal poisoning (e.g., arsenic or lead). True Leukonychia: This is the most common form of leukonychia and manifests as small white spots on the nails. In children and individuals who habitually bite or pick their nails, trauma to the nail matrix is a frequent cause. When white spots appear on one or a few nails, they typically resolve within approximately eight months, which is the time required for complete nail regrowth. However, if white spots are present on most or all nails for extended periods (months to years), this may indicate an underlying issue, such as zinc deficiency. Pathophysiology and Associated Conditions Leukonychia can be associated with systemic conditions, including: Kidney disease Liver disease Causes of Leukonychia The potential causes of leukonychia are numerous and include: Laboratory tests to evaluate liver and kidney function may also be performed. During the physical examination, the nails will be closely inspected for the characteristic white discoloration, and the findings will be compared to dermatological references, such as those found in dermatology atlases. Treatment If leukonychia is determined to be caused by a zinc deficiency, treatment may involve dietary modifications to include zinc-rich foods or the administration of zinc supplements.
